title: Swapping Nodes in a Linked List
prompt:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list and an integer `k`, swap the values of the `k`th node from the beginning and the `k`th node from the end (both 1-indexed), then return the head of the list.

The list is given as an array (e.g. `[1,2,3,4,5]` represents `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> null`). The starter code includes helpers to convert between the array and a linked-list node — build the actual list, swap the two nodes' values, then convert back to an array to return.
constraints: The number of nodes is n
hints: You don't know n in advance without a pass through the list — but you can find both target nodes in a single additional pass using two pointers.
First pass: walk k steps from head to locate the kth node from the beginning; keep a reference to it.

Second pass idea without recomputing length: once you're at the kth node from the start, start a second pointer at head and advance both it and a pointer from the kth node together until the leading one reaches the end — the trailing pointer lands on the kth node from the end.

solution.approach: Walk a pointer k steps from head to find the kth node from the beginning; call it `first`. Then, to find the kth node from the end without knowing the list's length ahead of time, start a second pointer `second` at head and advance both `first` (continuing from where it left off) and `second` together, one step at a time, until `first` reaches the last node. At that point `second` is exactly k nodes from the end, since the gap between the two pointers has stayed fixed at (original position of first) the whole time. Swap the two nodes' `.val` fields (an O(1) fix once both are located) rather than rewiring pointers.
